extracted.intended_audience: broadcast and digital journalists, newsroom leaders and members of RTDNA
extracted.subtask_description: A code of ethics for broadcast and digital news practitioners that sets principles and specific standards for reporting, newsgathering, editorial independence, transparency, and accountability to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalism's obligation to the public / public interest priority
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism’s obligation is to the public; journalism places the public’s interests ahead of commercial, political and personal interests and empowers audiences to make informed decisions rather than telling them what to believe or how to feel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle underpins editorial choices; coverage, selection, production and delivery should prioritize public interest over outside interests or personal agendas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical decision-making throughout the journalistic process
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethical decision-making should occur at every step of the journalistic process, including story selection, newsgathering, production, presentation and delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should apply ethical reasoning continuously and treat ethical practice as a learned skill that improves with study, diligence and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek diverse and opposing opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners of ethical journalism seek diverse and even opposing opinions to reach better conclusions that can be clearly explained, effectively defended, or when appropriate, revisited and revised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively pursue multiple perspectives; be transparent about what is included and omitted in coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth and accuracy above all
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth and accuracy are the primary obligations of journalism — facts should take precedence over producing a good story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalism requires verifying information, providing relevant context, telling the rest of the story and acknowledging important missing information rather than merely reporting claims or remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification and contextualization
rubrics_metrics.description: Never cut corners factually: verify claims and provide relevant context so reporting does not oversimplify complex issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scarce resources, deadline pressure, and competition do not excuse failing to verify or oversimplifying material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge omissions and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Responsible reporting is clear about what it omits as well as what it includes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When significant relevant information cannot fit into a report, disclose those limits so audiences understand the scope of reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heightened accuracy when stories trend or go viral
rubrics_metrics.description: "Trending," "going viral" or social-media urgency increases the need for strict accuracy standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increased public attention raises—not lowers—the obligation to verify and contextualize information before publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Update and correct stories over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts change over time; responsible reporting includes updating stories and amending archival versions to become more accurate and avoid misinforming searchers who find outdated material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make corrections promptly and amend archives when necessary so historical content does not continue to mislead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on deceptive newsgathering (with narrow exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deception in newsgathering, including surreptitious recording, conflicts with journalism’s commitment to truth and is generally unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surreptitious tactics are justified only when stories of great significance cannot be adequately told otherwise, and any creative liberties must be clearly explained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about source anonymity and staging
rubrics_metrics.description: Anonymity of sources deprives the audience of important relevant information; staging, dramatization and other alterations — even when labeled — can confuse or fool audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anonymity undermines audience evaluation of credibility; staging or dramatization must be rare, clearly explained, and only used when absolutely necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenge assumptions and reject stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism should challenge assumptions, reject stereotypes and illuminate ignorance where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters must avoid perpetuating bias and should scrutinize commonly held beliefs rather than repeating them uncritically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist false dichotomies and consider alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethical journalism resists false dichotomies (either/or, always/never thinking) and considers a range of alternatives between extremes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame stories to reflect nuance; avoid forcing complex issues into simplistic binaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence from conflicting influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Independence from commercial, political and other interests that conflict with the public interest is essential; journalists should resist influences internal and external to media companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that full insulation may be impossible but treat independence as a core ideal that guides decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency to allow public assessment of credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparency provides the public means to assess credibility and determine who deserves trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain relationships, funding, sponsorship and relevant ties so audiences can evaluate potential conflicts; transparency requires reflection and openness, not excuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure is necessary but not sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledging sponsor-provided content, commercial concerns or political relationships is essential, but disclosure alone does not entitle lowering standards of fairness or truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure must be accompanied by equitable editorial decisions; it cannot be used to exclude important perspectives from coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold the powerful accountable, including journalists and employers
rubrics_metrics.description: The tradition of holding the powerful accountable applies equally to powerful journalists and the organizations that employ them; profiting from secrecy is hypocrisy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat internal and external power with the same accountability standards applied to other subjects of reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Own errors and correct them promptly and prominently
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethical journalism requires owning errors, correcting them promptly and giving corrections as much prominence as the original error had.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrections should not be buried or minimized; be transparent about mistakes and remedial steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial endorsements are incompatible with journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial endorsements compromise credibility and are incompatible with journalism because they conflate editorial content with paid promotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content selection and production must serve audiences, not advertisers or paid promoters; avoid endorsements tied to a familiar face, voice, or name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit political activity and advocacy that undercuts independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Political activity and active advocacy by journalists can undercut real or perceived independence and should be limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists retain citizenship rights but should be aware that public exercise of those rights may call into question impartiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid acceptance of gifts or special treatment that create conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance of gifts or special treatment not available to the general public creates conflicts of interest and erodes independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions include ordinary access or credentials traditionally granted to working journalists; declines professional courtesies that could be perceived as enticements or rewards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution and plagiarism avoidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribution is essential; using someone else’s work without attribution or permission is plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always credit contributors and sources; attribution helps audiences evaluate content and acknowledges contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept responsibility and open processes to scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism accepts responsibility, articulates its reasons and opens its processes to public scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to explain editorial choices and invite accountability rather than concealment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize harm and consider vulnerable stakeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimizing harm, particularly to vulnerable individuals, should be a consideration in every editorial and ethical decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider consequences of newsgathering and dissemination — including those never made public — and give special consideration to children, victims, vulnerable adults and those inexperienced with media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance privacy and fair trial concerns against public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Preserving privacy and protecting the right to a fair trial are important concerns that must be balanced against the importance or urgency of reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These protections are not primary missions of journalism but deserve careful weighing in editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue truth and report rather than withhold for convenience
rubrics_metrics.description: The right to publish does not mean it is always right to do so, but journalism’s obligation is to pursue truth and report, not to withhold it as a default.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid shirking difficult or sensitive stories merely to avoid controversy; leaving such stories to non-journalists can be a disservice to the public.
